Red is where Polish was the mother tongue. The western half of interwar Poland is almost solid. The eastern half is red islands in a black sea — and that map is why Poland's borders moved west in 1945.

a thread 🧵🗺️

1/ The numbers under it come from the census of 9 December 1931 — Poland's second, covering almost 32 million people. It asked for mother tongue rather than nationality. That single choice shapes everything you're looking at.

2/ The national result: 68.9% Polish, 13.9% Ukrainian, about 10% Jewish by language, 3.1% Belarusian, 2.3% German. A state that thought of itself as a nation-state was, on its own figures, roughly a third not Polish.

3/ The red islands in the east are towns. Lwów and Wilno were Polish-speaking cities sitting inside Ukrainian- and Belarusian-speaking countryside. In the same province, the market square and the villages around it answered differently.

4/ The census also allowed "tutejszy" — local, from here. In Polesia more than 707,000 people chose it. They weren't dodging the question. A national label simply wasn't the first thing they'd have said about themselves.

5/ Historians treat the figures as official but shaky. Tadeusz Piotrowski calls the census unreliable for measuring ethnicity, and critics note Ukrainian and Ruthenian were tallied as separate languages — splitting one group into two.

6/ Whether that was deliberate has never been settled. The pre-war census chief was later quoted by communist sources admitting officials were told to undercount minorities in the east. The admission itself has never been produced.

7/ After 1945 the argument stopped mattering. The Soviet border took the black half, and more than a million Poles were moved west into formerly German land. Poland became the monolingual country this map says it wasn't.

Follow @forummapping for more maps like this.
